hook_text: You can't count atoms. So chemists weigh them instead — with one genius trick.
clip_script: Atoms are absurdly small. No balance on Earth weighs one molecule. Yet chemical reactions happen molecule by molecule. Chemistry needs a way to count particles while weighing grams. The solution is the same trick shops use: count in bulk units. Eggs come in dozens; chemists count in moles — and one mole is simply a fixed, enormous number of particles: six comma zero two times ten to the twenty-three. Why that bizarre number? Because it is chosen to make the arithmetic beautiful: one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative molecular mass.
visual_style: Zoom from a single invisible molecule out to an egg carton, then to a balance reading 44 g as a mole counter ticks to 6,02×10²³.
pacing: Slow cosmic zoom, quick dozen analogy, satisfying number landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run the 8,8 gram problem across the mole map.
